meta.date: ~600 BC (in vision, from the valley of Lemuel)

world_behind.title: Iron yokes were prophetic hardware
world_behind.text: The church that "yoketh them with a yoke of iron" (v. 5) borrows Jeremiah's stage prop: in Lehi's own decade, Jeremiah wore a wooden yoke to prophesy servitude, and when it was broken, the Lord promised yokes of iron instead (Jer. 28:13–14). Nephi's hearers knew the image as recent street theater with a hard ending.

cites.quote: yoketh them with a yoke of iron

spans.text: yoketh them with a yoke of iron

world_behind.title: John saw kindred scenes
world_behind.text: Gold, scarlet, fine linen, harlots, war on the saints: the vision's portrait of corrupt religion shares its wardrobe with the woman of Revelation 17 and its violence with the beast of Revelation 13. Two seers, centuries apart, given the same iconography for the same enemy.

world_behind.title: The nameless voyagers
world_behind.text: The record never names the "man among the Gentiles" (v. 12) or the multitudes that follow; readers since the book's first edition have seen the discovery voyages and colonial migrations here, and the text's own restraint is worth keeping: it describes offices (wrought upon, delivered, prospered), not resumes.

cites.quote: man among the Gentiles

spans.text: man among the Gentiles

world_behind.title: What the book's journey looked like
world_behind.text: Between "the mouth of a Jew" and the modern Gentile reader lie a thousand years of copying, translating, canon disputes, and institutional custody. The vision compresses that transmission history into one image, a book passing "through the hands of the great and abominable church" (v. 28), and grieves what fell out along the way.

cites.quote: through the hands of the great and abominable church

spans.text: through the hands of the great and abominable church

world_behind.title: Israel preserved the book
world_behind.text: "it proceedeth out of the mouth of a Jew" (v. 23) is the vision's standing tribute: scripture's origin is Jewish speech, prophecy, and scribal labor. The record's later, sterner word to Gentiles who despise the Jews while living off their book (2 Ne. 29:4–5) begins in this verse's respect.

cites.quote: it proceedeth out of the mouth of a Jew

spans.text: it proceedeth out of the mouth of a Jew

world_behind.title: Many waters meant the ocean
world_behind.text: In Israel's poetry the sea is vastness and peril: they that go down to the sea in ships see the Lord's wonders in the deep (Ps. 107:23–24). The vision makes the ocean its stage twice over: first the divider protecting the remnant, then the highway the Spirit sends the Gentiles across.

words.text: The Spirit "came down and wrought upon the man" (v. 12): worked him, the way metal or dough is worked. The discovery of the new world is told entirely in this verb's grammar: history's famous crossings appear as the product of a Workman shaping willing material, and the workers themselves go unnamed.

cites.quote: came down and wrought upon the man

spans.text: came down and wrought upon the man

words.text: The theft's effect on ordinary readers: "an exceedingly great many do stumble" (v. 29). Nobody in the verse rejects the gospel; they trip over its gaps. The word carries the vision's tenderness toward the Gentile centuries: their blindness is described as an injury done to them, not a crime done by them.

cites.quote: an exceedingly great many do stumble

spans.text: an exceedingly great many do stumble

phrases.text: The vision's strongest loathing word is aimed with care: at an institution defined by its founder (the devil, v. 6), its conduct (slays, tortures, binds, yokes, v. 5), and its inventoried desires, "the gold, and the silver, and the silks, and the scarlets" (v. 8), "the praise of the world" (v. 9). No nation or denomination is named, and chapter 14 will supply the control: two churches only, sorted by whom they fight. The category is moral conduct, not a congregation, and any institution in any era can walk into or out of it.

cites.quote: the gold, and the silver, and the silks, and the scarlets

spans.text: the gold, and the silver, and the silks, and the scarlets

cites.quote: the praise of the world

spans.text: the praise of the world

phrases.text: The ocean plays both of its parts in one panel: first the moat that "divided the Gentiles from the seed of my brethren" (v. 10), then the road the Spirit-driven ships cross. The same waters protect and deliver, depending on whose errand is on them; the vision's geography always answers to purpose.

cites.quote: divided the Gentiles from the seed of my brethren

spans.text: divided the Gentiles from the seed of my brethren

phrases.text: Three times in seven verses (v. 13, 16, 19) the colonizing Gentiles are described in exodus grammar. The record files the future migrations with Israel's founding story (captivity, crossing, deliverance by God's power) and thereby claims those Gentile descendants as characters inside covenant history, with covenant accountability coming (ch. 14).

phrases.term: proceedeth out of the mouth of a Jew
phrases.text: The Bible's birth certificate in the vision's language: not from an institution or a council but from a mouth: spoken prophecy, Jewish speech, before it was ever a book. The phrase gives the record its settled posture toward the Bible: filial respect for the people whose mouth it came from.

The famous pair names two different losses: plain things — clarity "unto the understanding of the children of men" (v. 29), scripture needing no guild to interpret — and precious things, the covenants and weightier promises. Plainness in this record is a kindness, and its theft is the vision's real crime scene. The vision's restoration program (v. 34–35, 40) promises both back, and the record the reader is holding presents itself as that program's instrument.

cites.quote: unto the understanding of the children of men

spans.text: unto the understanding of the children of men

phrases.term: the book of the Lamb of God
phrases.text: By the panel's end the wounded book has a new name, ownership restored by title. Whatever was taken in transit, the vision never lets the Bible stop belonging to the Lamb, and the last records come forth not to replace it but to "establish the truth of the first" (v. 40).

cites.quote: establish the truth of the first

spans.text: establish the truth of the first

verses.label: v. 1–9
verses.title: A portrait with no name on it
verses.text: Among the nations of the Gentiles the vision singles out one institution and identifies it three ways — founder, conduct, wants — while declining to name any nation or sect. What it does have a name for is its victims: "the saints of God" (v. 9). The portrait works as a mirror rather than a map, and mirrors are harder to argue with.

cites.quote: the saints of God

spans.text: the saints of God

verses.label: v. 10–12
verses.title: One man on many waters
verses.text: Between wrath on the remnant and multitudes to follow, the vision isolates a single Gentile, "separated from the seed of my brethren by the many waters" (v. 12), and moves him by the Spirit. World-changing history is shown as one wrought-upon man in a boat; the vision's scale of causes is never the world's.

cites.quote: separated from the seed of my brethren by the many waters

spans.text: separated from the seed of my brethren by the many waters

verses.label: v. 13–19
verses.title: Exodus of the Gentiles
verses.text: Out of captivity, across the water, humbled before the Lord, delivered from "their mother Gentiles" (v. 17): the colonial story told in Israel's founding grammar, with God's power the recurring actor. The record grants the future settlers a real deliverance and quietly sets the terms they will be judged by.

cites.quote: their mother Gentiles

spans.text: their mother Gentiles

verses.label: v. 20–29
verses.title: The book's hard journey
verses.text: A book among the prospering Gentiles; its origin "the fulness of the gospel of the Lord" (v. 24) from the mouth of a Jew; then the theft in transit (plain and precious things, and covenants, taken) and the wreckage: stumbling readers and a power vacuum Satan fills (v. 29). The vision mourns the Bible's wounds without ever mocking the book.

cites.quote: the fulness of the gospel of the Lord

spans.text: the fulness of the gospel of the Lord

verses.label: v. 30–33
verses.title: The neither-will-he-suffer clauses
verses.text: Three restraints in four verses: the Gentiles shall not destroy the remnant's mixture, the remnant shall not be wholly lost, the Gentiles shall not remain forever blind. Mercy is drawn as a fence around wrath, and the Lamb himself speaks the middle promise: "I will be merciful unto the Gentiles" (v. 33).

cites.quote: I will be merciful unto the Gentiles

spans.text: I will be merciful unto the Gentiles

verses.label: v. 34–37
verses.title: The restoration announced
verses.text: The Lamb will "manifest myself unto thy seed" (v. 35), who will write plain and precious things to come forth after the Gentile book. Verse 37 blesses the future workers — Zion-bringers with "the gift and the power of the Holy Ghost" (v. 37), and crowns them with Isaiah's runner: "how beautiful upon the mountains shall they be" (v. 37).

cites.quote: manifest myself unto thy seed

spans.text: manifest myself unto thy seed

cites.quote: the gift and the power of the Holy Ghost

spans.text: the gift and the power of the Holy Ghost

cites.quote: how beautiful upon the mountains shall they be

spans.text: how beautiful upon the mountains shall they be

verses.label: v. 38–42
verses.title: The records convince together
verses.text: Other books come forth, the last to "establish the truth of the first" (v. 40), and the two are promised a single destiny: "they both shall be established in one; for there is one God and one Shepherd over all the earth" (v. 41). The panel ends with order restored among peoples and testaments alike: "the last shall be first, and the first shall be last" (v. 42).

chapter.title: A book prophesying about books
chapter.text: The vision's third panel is textual history: where the Bible came from, what happened to it, and what will be written to rescue its readers. The record's deepest self-understanding is on display — it exists because of what this chapter says was lost, and the reader is holding the instrument verse 35 commissions.

chapter.title: Corruption identified by appetite
chapter.text: The abominable church is diagnosed by desires and deeds, never by name — and the next chapter's two-church taxonomy confirms the category is functional. The record hands no sect a weapon here; it hands every institution, its own descendants' included, a mirror.

chapter.title: The Bible honored as a wounded parent
chapter.text: From a Jewish mouth, in purity, through rough custody, to every Gentile nation: the record's account of the Bible is grief and gratitude together, and its own mission is framed as filial — to establish the truth of the first, not to compete with it.

chapter.title: Gentile history inside covenant history
chapter.text: Discovery, colonization, and deliverance from the mother nations are told in exodus grammar with God as actor. The record refuses to leave the Gentiles outside the story — which also means they do not get to stay outside its accountability.

chapter.title: Mercy fences every wrath scene
chapter.text: The panel's darkest material is bracketed by neither-will-he-suffer clauses and closed by the Lamb's own mercy speech. Even the vision's judgment passages are structured as covenant restraint — wrath bounded, remnant kept, blindness scheduled to end.

chapter.title: The widening circles complete their sweep
chapter.text: Christ (ch. 11), the family's nations (ch. 12), and now all nations and their books. When chapter 15 shows the brothers refusing to ask about any of this, the reader will know the full size of what they declined.

applications.title: Run the desires audit
applications.text: The vision identifies corrupt religion by what it wants. Turn the instrument on your own practice of faith: list what you actually seek from your religion this month — comfort, standing, wealth, praise, or the saints' God — and let the list correct itself.

applications.title: Read the Bible as a survivor
applications.text: Study it with the tenderness owed a wounded book: gratitude for the Jewish mouths and hands that carried it, patience with its hard places, and the restoration's witnesses open beside it to supply what transit cost.

applications.title: Keep things plain
applications.text: The vision's villains complicated scripture until ordinary people stumbled. Whatever you teach — class, family, testimony — practice plainness as a form of kindness: one true thing, reachable words, no guild required.

applications.title: Claim the verse 37 blessing on purpose
applications.text: The promise is for those who seek to bring forth Zion, not those who admire it. Pick one act this month that is unambiguously Zion-work (a name to the temple, a neighbor served, peace published in your own house) and do it as a claim on the gift the verse attaches.

applications.title: Let the books establish each other
applications.text: Build your study so the records corroborate: read the Bible and this record on the same doctrine in the same week, and write one sentence on what each establishes in the other. Testimony built on two witnesses holds in weather that topples one.

questions.text: Which of the church of desire's appetites (wealth, finery, indulgence, applause) currently has the easiest access to me?
Where in my own family's crossing story did the Spirit work on ordinary, nameless people, and have I told it that way?
Which plain thing have I made complicated, and who has stumbled on my version of it?
Do I extend to blinded people the vision's courtesy, injured rather than indicted, or do I grade them as if they had what was taken from them?
What did I actually do toward bringing forth Zion in the last month, in deeds a stranger could point to?
Where am I assuming a first place that the last-first inversion should make me hold more loosely?
